passages.t: Zophar: God exacts less than you deserve
passages.happening:
‘Then Zophar the Naamathite replied’ (verse 1). “Should this stream of words go unanswered and such a speaker be vindicated?” (verse 2). Job has babbled and scoffed, he says, and claimed that his teaching is sound and that he is pure in God's sight.

“But if only God would speak and open His lips against you, and disclose to you the secrets of wisdom, for true wisdom has two sides. Know then that God exacts from you less than your iniquity deserves” (verses 5-6).
passages.hearers:
Zophar is the third friend, from a place called Naamah, probably somewhere in the region of Edom or northern Arabia, though its location is unknown. He speaks for the first time, and he is the most impatient. He does what the others only hinted at. He tells Job flatly that he is guilty.

His case, in the form he would sign, is this. God's wisdom has a hidden side that Job cannot see. If Job could see it, he would know that his suffering is not too much but too little for what he has done, and he would stop protesting and turn to God.

There is an irony here. Zophar wishes God would speak and set Job straight. Much later God does speak, and his rebuke falls on the friends (42:7).

Two sides, in verse 6, is a difficult phrase. It probably means that real wisdom has a hidden dimension beyond what is seen. The book agrees, and the hidden side of Job's story is one Zophar cannot see.
passages.later: A psalm says a true thing much like Zophar's: “He has not dealt with us according to our sins or repaid us according to our iniquities” (Psalm 103:10). The psalm says it in praise of mercy, not as a verdict on a sufferer.
passages.hard:
Is Zophar right that God gives people less than their sins deserve?

As a general statement, many biblical writers would agree that God does not treat people as their sins deserve (Psalm 103:10), and Christian teaching holds that every good gift is mercy. So the sentence holds a true idea. What makes it false here is its use. Zophar says it to a man God has called blameless, as an explanation of his losses. That means he is accusing Job of hidden sins worse even than his suffering.

The book shows that this is exactly wrong. Job's suffering has a cause Zophar knows nothing about (chapters 1 and 2), and God later rebukes the friends (42:7). Many readers draw the lesson that a true teaching can be spoken in a false way, and that speaking it to a sufferer as a verdict on their life fails both truth and love. No one may say to a person in pain that they deserve worse.
passages.asks: Zophar spoke of mercy in a way that wounded. Ask whether you have ever used a true teaching to hurt someone. And ask how the same truth would sound if it were spoken in praise instead of as a charge.

passages.t: Higher than the heavens, deeper than Sheol
passages.happening:
“Can you fathom the deep things of God or discover the limits of the Almighty?” (verse 7). They are higher than the heavens and deeper than Sheol, longer than the earth and wider than the sea.

If God imprisons or calls a court, who can stop him? He knows the deceit of men, and he takes note of wrong. “But a witless man can no more become wise than the colt of a wild donkey can be born a man!” (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
Zophar's short hymn measures God's depths by the four directions of the world: up to the heavens, down to Sheol, out across the earth and the sea. It is some of the most beautiful poetry in the friends' speeches, and it anticipates what God himself will say in chapter 38.

That makes the irony sharper. Zophar says no one can fathom God, and in the same breath he claims to know exactly what God is doing in Job's life.

Verse 12 sounds like a folk saying, and it is meant to sting. The wild donkey was a byword for the untamed and stubborn. Zophar is saying that a fool like Job is about as likely to become wise as a wild donkey is to be born human.
passages.later: The wild donkey was a picture of the untamable from the beginning: Ishmael ‘will be a wild donkey of a man’, the angel tells Hagar (Genesis 16:12).
passages.asks: Zophar praised the depth of God and then claimed to see to the bottom of it. Ask whether you are more certain about what God is doing in other people's lives than in your own. And ask what it would mean to leave God's depths deep.

passages.t: Lift up your hands, and your life will be bright
passages.happening:
“As for you, if you direct your heart and lift up your hands to Him, if you put away the iniquity in your hand, and allow no injustice to dwell in your tents, then indeed you will lift up your face without shame” (verses 13-15).

Job will forget his misery, ‘recalling it only as waters gone by’ (verse 16). His life will be brighter than noonday, and its darkness like the morning. He will lie down in safety, and many will seek his favor. “But the eyes of the wicked will fail, and escape will elude them; they will hope for their last breath” (verse 20).
passages.hearers:
Lifting up the hands describes a common posture of prayer: standing with open palms raised toward heaven, a gesture of appeal and of empty hands before God. Putting iniquity out of the hand plays on that picture. Hands raised in prayer should be clean.

The call is a sound description of turning back to God, and the promises are beautiful. The speech ends like Eliphaz's and Bildad's, with a picture of the restored penitent, and then a warning about the wicked.

It becomes cruel only because of what Zophar assumes. Repentance is the right counsel for a sin. Zophar offers it to a man whose suffering is not the fruit of sin, and he ends by hinting that Job may be among the wicked whose only hope is their last breath.
passages.asks: Zophar's promises were lovely and misplaced. Ask whether you have ever offered someone a cure for a fault they did not have. And ask what you would say to a friend in trouble if you could not assume anything about why it came.
